note: Source says light troops furnished with armour; candidate vaguely says equipment.
replacement: While the Chians were busy with this, toward the end of the same summer a force sailed from Athens in forty-eight ships, some of them transports. It consisted of a thousand Athenian heavy infantry, fifteen hundred Argives (five hundred of them light troops equipped with armor by the Athenians) and a thousand men from the allies. Phrynichus, Onomacles and Scironides commanded it. It put in at Samos, crossed over, and encamped at Miletus. The Milesians then came out against the Athenians and their allies, with eight hundred heavy infantry, the Peloponnesians who had arrived with Chalcideus, some foreign mercenaries of Tissaphernes, and Tissaphernes himself with his cavalry. The Argives, on their own wing, charged forward with the careless disdain of men advancing against Ionians who would never withstand their attack, and the Milesians defeated them, killing little short of three hundred. The Athenians, for their part, first defeated the Peloponnesians and drove the barbarians and the rabble of the army before them. They did not engage the Milesians, who had seen the Argives routed and retreated into the town. The Athenians then crowned their victory by grounding their arms right under the walls of Miletus. So in this battle the Ionians on both sides overcame the Dorians: the Athenians beat the Peloponnesians opposed to them, and the Milesians beat the Argives. After setting up a trophy, the Athenians prepared to build a wall around the town, which stood on an isthmus. They thought that if they gained Miletus, the other towns would easily come over to them.

note: Name served as Onamacles was changed to Onomacles.
replacement: The same winter the Athenians at Samos were joined by thirty-five more vessels from home under Charminus, Strombichides and Euctemon. They called in their squadron at Chios and all the rest, intending to blockade Miletus with their navy and to send a fleet and an army against Chios, and they drew lots for the respective services. They carried out this plan. Strombichides, Onamacles and Euctemon, to whom Chios fell by lot, sailed against it with thirty ships and a part of the thousand heavy infantry who had been at Miletus, carried in transports. The rest stayed at Samos with seventy-four ships, held command of the sea, and advanced on Miletus.

note: Source does not say what was fortified; candidate adds the referent “it” (Lesbos).
replacement: Meanwhile the Athenian armament, sailing around Corycus, fell in with three Chian warships off Arginus and gave immediate chase. A great storm came on, and the Chians took refuge in the harbor with difficulty. The three Athenian vessels that were furthest forward in the pursuit were wrecked and thrown up near the city of Chios, and their crews were killed or taken prisoner. The rest of the Athenian fleet took refuge in the harbor called Phoenicus, under Mount Mimas, and afterwards put into Lesbos from there and prepared for the work of fortification.
